# LITs with `tags` `databases`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds what the Anthology of the SOTA does not: reading whose subject no anthology topic can hold. The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Databases and data structures** — how stored data is organized so that it can be found and kept current — physical database design and index selection, materialized views and the choice of which answers to precompute, adaptive and self-organizing structures, lower bounds on lookup, caching and paging; and the cost of organizing ahead of use against organizing in use. Read for itself, not as ML practice: learned indexes and other machine-learning approaches go to the anthology (ADR-045).

| [LIT-1083](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1083.md) | An Efficient, Cost-Driven Index Selection Tool for Microsoft SQL Server | Chaudhuri and Narasayya (1997), VLDB '97. The AutoAdmin tool picks at most k indexes (single- or two-column, clustered or not) for a given workload of SQL statements, minimising the unweighted sum of the optimizer's estimated costs of those statements, with hypothetical ("what-if") indexes made visible to the optimizer by loading their statistics into the catalog. On five TPC-D workloads this cut running time to 10–24% of a baseline, with estimated-cost quality 0–7% worse, and Greedy(2, 4) matched the exhaustive optimum on four of five workloads and was within 1% on the fifth. The extremes themselves show the overheads are not symmetric: the space-minimal design is also update-minimal, and the read-minimal design keeps updates at 2.0, so the clean conflicts are read against space and update against both. | [LIT-1090](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1090.md) | Database Cracking | Idreos, Kersten and Manegold (2007), CIDR. Database cracking builds an index as a by-product of answering range queries. Each select partitions, in place, the part of a copy of the column that the query had to touch, so that the qualifying values lie contiguously, and records the new boundaries in a small tree; later queries touch only the pieces at the edges of their range, so per-query cost falls as the column is split into more pieces. On a 10^7-value column under uniformly random range queries, the first cracking select costs 0.38 s against 0.27 s for a scan and about 3.3 s for sort-then-search, and cumulative cost stays below sorting's until about 10^5 queries, after which upfront sorting wins. The authors claim that only ranges of past interest get organized, but every experiment uses uniformly random ranges, so that claim is not measured; there is no cost model, no rule for when a reorganization is worth making, and updates, concurrency and out-of-memory data are left as open problems. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the paper as published in the CIDR 2007 proceedings (cidrdb.org/cidr2007/papers/cidr07p07.pdf, which redirects to www.cidrdb.org; printed pp. 68–78, CC BY 2.5). Worth reading as the founding account of indexing by query: each range select partitions in place the part of a column copy it had to scan, records the new boundaries in an AVL tree, and so makes later queries touch only the pieces at the edges of their range. On 10^7 values under uniformly random ranges the first cracking query costs 0.38 s against 0.27 s for a scan and about 3.3 s for sort-then-search, and upfront sorting overtakes cracking only after about 10^5 queries. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it shows sorting as amortized search in a literal sense, with a measured break-even, but gives no cost model and no rule for when a reorganization is worth making; the claim that only ranges of interest get organized is not tested, since every workload is uniform. For [CASE-094](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-094.md) the analogy holds for organizing as a by-product of retrieval and fails on the mechanism: cracking splits everything it searched around an ordered key, and reorganizes on every query whatever the chance of reuse, where the case sets aside only the found brick, and only when it is rare and often used. |

Worth reading as the general statement of view selection: AND-OR view graphs with query and update frequencies, and an objective of frequency-weighted query cost plus update-frequency-weighted maintenance cost under a space budget, with greedy guarantees of 1 − 1/e of the optimal benefit when space may overrun. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it gives the joint objective in form: reuse against per-update upkeep under capacity. | [LIT-1092](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1092.md) | Selection of Views to Materialize Under a Maintenance Cost Constraint | Gupta and Mumick (1999), ICDT '99. Gupta and Mumick choose views to materialize so as to minimize frequency-weighted query cost subject to a cap S on total maintenance time, the sum over chosen views of update frequency times a per-update maintenance cost that depends on which other views are stored. Because storing one view can make another cheaper to maintain, benefit per unit of maintenance is not monotone and the single-view greedy of earlier work can be arbitrarily bad. For OR view graphs (each view computed from one other, as in data cubes) a greedy that adds whole "inverted tree sets" gets at least 1 − 1/e (63%) of the benefit of an optimal solution that may use as much maintenance as the greedy did, the greedy using up to 2S, assuming no inverted-tree piece of the optimum alone exceeds S (Theorem 1, unproved here); without that assumption it gets half the optimum's benefit per unit of maintenance (Theorem 2). Each greedy stage enumerates exponentially many sets in general; for general AND-OR graphs there is only an exact A* search with exponential worst case. Upkeep is a budget, not a term traded against query savings; build cost, storage and staleness are not modelled, and the experiments are on random graphs of 10 to 25 nodes. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' PostScript copy on Stanford InfoLab's papers server (infolab.stanford.edu/pub/papers/update.ps, 18 pages, dated 8 October 1998, the ICDT '99 camera-ready, not the 2005 TKDE journal version; not compared with Springer's typeset pages). Worth reading as the first view-selection result that budgets maintenance time instead of space, and for its demonstration that upkeep is not additive: storing one view can make others cheaper to maintain, so benefit per unit of maintenance is not monotone and single-view greedy can be arbitrarily bad. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it shows upkeep priced as a budget, U(M) = Σ update frequency × per-update maintenance cost given the other stored views, with query cost the only objective; build cost, storage and staleness are not modelled (every view is refreshed in a nightly batch). Its guarantee answers the open problem of [LIT-1091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1091.md) only for OR view graphs: 1 − 1/e of an optimum's benefit while using up to twice the budget, under an assumption on the optimum, or half the optimum's benefit per unit of maintenance without it, with the theorems stated but not proved and a greedy whose stages are exponential in general (including on data cubes). General AND-OR graphs get only an exact A* search. It does not close the question, and comes no closer to a joint cost model than [LIT-1095](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1095.md). |
| [LIT-1093](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1093.md) | Amortized efficiency of list update and paging rules | Sleator and Tarjan (1985), CACM 28(2). For a list searched sequentially from the front, where reaching the i-th item costs i, moving each accessed item to the front costs at most twice what any other rule costs on the same sequence, including rules that know the whole sequence in advance (four times, counting move-to-front's own moves), with no probabilistic assumption. A fixed list sorted by access frequency, and the transpose and frequency-count rules, are not within any constant factor of that. Rearranging ahead of need never pays in this model (Theorem 3). For paging, where only a small fast memory is cheap, no rule that cannot see the future can do better in the worst case than n/(n − n_MIN + 1) times the offline optimum MIN, and LRU and FIFO attain that bound up to an additive n_MIN; with equal memories the ratio is the memory size. The model is a single linear list (or a two-level memory) with uniform items and access cost depending only on position; it says nothing about partitions, bins or search that is not a scan. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the scan of the published CACM article (pp. 202–208, with ACM's running heads and copyright line) on Sleator's CMU page (www.cs.cmu.edu/~sleator/papers/amortized-efficiency.pdf); the ACM Digital Library's open-access PDF refused direct requests from this environment. Worth reading as the founding worst-case comparison of an online rule with the best offline one: on a sequentially scanned list where reaching position i costs i, move-to-front costs at most twice what any rule in the class costs on the same sequence, even one that knows the future (four times counting its own moves), while a fixed list sorted by frequency, transpose and frequency count are not within any constant; and for paging no online rule beats n/(n − n_MIN + 1) times Belady's MIN, a bound LRU and FIFO meet up to an additive n_MIN. | [LIT-1094](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1094.md) | Implementing data cubes efficiently | Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman (1996), SIGMOD '96. Treats a data cube's group-by queries as a lattice in which a query can be answered from any stored ancestor, prices a query at the number of rows of the smallest materialized ancestor, and chooses which views to precompute. Choosing k views to maximize the total reduction in query cost (the "benefit") is NP-complete; a greedy rule that adds the view of largest marginal benefit gets at least 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ (e−1)/e ≈ 63% of the optimal benefit, a bound that is tight, holds unchanged with query-frequency weights, and weakens to 0.63 − f under a space budget when no view takes more than a fraction f of it. The cost of building views is represented only by their size, maintenance and updates are not modelled, the data are static, and the bound is on benefit, not on query cost. On TPC-D data the greedy order reaches nearly the minimum total query time with five views and barely more space than the base view. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the authors' 25-page version on Stanford InfoLab's papers server (infolab.stanford.edu/pub/papers/cube.ps, TeX run of 8 January 1996), not the SIGMOD typesetting, which the ACM Digital Library refused (403); the two were not compared. Worth reading as the standard source on choosing which precomputed answers to store when each query is answered from its cheapest stored ancestor: the lattice of group-by views, the linear cost model (rows of the ancestor scanned), NP-completeness, and a greedy rule whose total benefit, the saving against storing the base view alone, is at least 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ (e−1)/e ≈ 63% of the optimum for a budget of k views, tight, unchanged with fixed query frequencies, and only 0.63 − f under a space budget when no view exceeds a fraction f of it. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) and [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it shows the precomputed-answer term the four earlier readings lacked, with a stored answer's value counted over every query it serves and marginal on what is already stored (sharpening [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md)'s break-even); it does not price build cost (space is a proxy), upkeep or staleness (the data are static and derived answers exact), timing or deadlines, uncertain workloads, or the medium of retrieval, so it is a model of the speed bugs only in naming the category, an analogy with one usable term for filed arguments, silent on the bias of reused inferences, and not about LEGO bins. |
| [LIT-1095](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1095.md) | An Online Approach to Physical Design Tuning | Bruno and Chaudhuri (2007), ICDE. An always-on index tuner for SQL Server. It keeps, for each candidate or existing index, the running sum of what each query would have saved with it (what-if optimizer estimates, with update costs counted as losses). It creates an index once that sum has risen by the index's build cost above its lowest point, and drops it once the sum has fallen by the build cost from its highest point. For one index with no space limit, the authors call this 3-competitive against the optimal schedule that knows the workload in advance. The proof only gives a workload on which the ratio approaches 3, and the paper cites no competitive-analysis work, ski rental included. The general case (many interacting indexes and a storage limit) uses heuristics with no guarantee. All costs in the experiments are optimizer estimates, on synthetic and TPC-H workloads. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the accepted-version PDF that Microsoft Research's publication page for the paper links (www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2007/01/continuous.pdf, 10 pp., no IEEE pagination). The authors were both at MSR; Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar list no open copy. Worth reading as the first model in the record that prices organizing ahead and organizing on demand on one schedule. It has a one-time build cost that depends on what is already built, per-statement savings, upkeep as the cost of update statements, a space limit, and a workload known only up to now. Its online rule builds an index once the benefit missed since the last low point equals the build cost, and drops it once the loss since the last high point equals the build cost. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it shows that the rule is rent-or-buy in structure but cites no competitive-analysis work, ski rental or Karlin et al. included. Its "three-competitive" result covers one index with no space limit, and is supported only by an example where the ratio approaches 3. By a check of my own it fails when a single statement's saving is large next to the build cost. The general case with space and interacting indexes is heuristic, dropping is free, there is no staleness or deadline, and all costs are optimizer estimates. For [CASE-094](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-094.md) it endorses making a bin at once when the bin costs almost nothing, and adds a matching rule for removing one. For [CLAIM-307](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-307.md) it replaces "carve when retrieval fails" with "carve when the extra search already spent equals the bin's cost": a cumulative-cost criterion with no deadline. |
| [LIT-1096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1096.md) | Competitive snoopy caching | Karlin, Manasse, Rudolph and Sleator (1988), Algorithmica 3. For a shared-bus multiprocessor whose caches can either keep a replicated block (and pay one bus cycle for every write to it) or drop it (and pay p to fetch it again if it is read), the paper gives counter-based on-line algorithms whose total bus cost on every request sequence is at most twice that of the best off-line algorithm, and proves that no deterministic on-line algorithm can guarantee better than 2. The rule is: drop a copy once the writes it has caused since it was last read have cost as much as refetching it. With a third option (reading or writing through without fetching) the lower bound rises to 3, and the algorithm given is 3-competitive ignoring writebacks, 4 counting them; with associative caches the bound becomes the paging ratio. The paper never names rent-or-buy or ski rental; its rent is upkeep paid on an idle copy, and its purchase is the refetch after dropping, the reverse orientation of building a bin. Costs are fixed constants, the guarantees are worst case only, and the authors call the practical significance "unclear". | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 (NOTE for this LIT) from a scan of the published Algorithmica article (pp. 79–119, Springer-Verlag copyright line) posted among the reading handouts of MIT course 6.896, Spring 2004 (courses.csail.mit.edu/6.896/spring04/class/www/handouts/papers/snoopy-cache.pdf); no author or repository copy was found (Unpaywall and OpenAlex: closed; not on Sleator's CMU or Karlin's UW pages). Worth reading as the first competitive analysis of a rent-or-buy decision: a cache keeping a shared block pays 1 per write to keep its copy current, or drops it and pays p to fetch it again if it reads; dropping once the writes charged since the last read have cost p is within 2 of the off-line optimum on every sequence (Theorem 4.1), and no deterministic on-line rule does better (Theorem 3.1); with a third option the bound rises to 3 (Theorem 3.3). The paper states the principle generally (change state when the extra cost of staying equals the cost of changing) but never names rent-or-buy or ski rental, and its instance is the decision to stop maintaining a copy, the mirror of building a bin. For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) and [CASE-094](../../../record/cases.d/CASE-094.md) it gives a worst-case rule for when a bin pays without knowing future use: make it when the extra search already spent equals its cost; for [CLAIM-303](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-303.md) it shows that a recurrence count weighted by reconstruction cost is, in the worst case, the right criterion and within 2, and that the second-occurrence rule is that rule only when filing costs about one reconstruction; for [QUESTION-095](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-095.md) it prices upkeep against re-retrieval and nothing on precomputation or staleness, which it forbids rather than prices. |
| [LIT-1097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1097.md) | Should Tables Be Sorted? | Yao (1981), JACM 28(3). For storing a set of n keys from a universe {1,…,m} in a table so that the membership query (is x in S?) is answered with the fewest worst-case adaptive probes, Yao proves that when the table cells may hold only keys of S or a bounded number of pointer symbols, sorted order with binary search (⌈lg(n+1)⌉ probes) is optimal once m exceeds a Ramsey-number threshold N(n, p, q), whatever the arrangement rule, table size or hashing scheme. The threshold is astronomically large, and for small universes sorted order is beaten (one probe suffices for m = 3 with n = 2, and for m ≤ 2n − 2 with n > 2). The optimality also fails as soon as one cell may hold an arbitrary value from the universe: with a single extra "directory" cell, two probes suffice for m ≥ 2^{16n²}. Only query cost is counted; building the table is free and unconstrained, so the paper says nothing about the cost of arranging or about trading arrangement cost against lookups. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the published Journal of the ACM version (28(3), pp. 615–628), which ACM serves free (OpenAlex/Unpaywall: bronze) but refused to this environment with 403, fetched instead as the copy on a University of Maryland course page (www.cs.umd.edu/users/gasarch/COURSES/858/S13/tables.pdf) and compared with the author's Stanford report STAN-CS-79-753 (i.stanford.edu/pub/cstr/reports/cs/tr/79/753/CS-TR-79-753.pdf), which has the same results. Worth reading as the paper that set up what is now called the cell-probe model, with lookup cost counted as the worst-case number of cells read and arrangement and search strategy left arbitrary: for static membership, sorted order with binary search (⌈lg(n+1)⌉ probes) is optimal once the key space exceeds a Ramsey-number threshold, provided cells hold only stored keys or pointer symbols; it is beaten for small key spaces (one probe for m ≤ 2n − 2), and for large ones as soon as one cell may hold an encoded value (two probes for m ≥ 2^{16n²}). For [QUESTION-114](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-114.md) it shows that "founding cell-probe paper" holds but "when storage in sorted order beats other arrangements" does not as worded: the theorem says nothing beats sorting under a no-encoding restriction for huge universes, and the rest of the paper shows other arrangements beating it. It counts lookup probes only; building the arrangement is free, so it bears nothing on whether sorting is amortized search or on the cost of organising set against lookups later. |
